list.listitem: Cognitive behavioral therapy is the recommended initial treatment for patients with chronic insomnia. A

Sedative hypnotics (zolpidem, ramelteon, zaleplon, eszopiclone) as well as dual orexin receptor antagonists (lemborexant, suvorexant, daridorexant) are moderately effective in the short term, but also have adverse effects such as depression and rebound insomnia. A
Indications for polysomnography include suspected obstructive sleep apnea or periodic limb movement disorder. C

background.definition: Insomnia is the inability to fall asleep or remain asleep. The National Sleep Foundation defines sleep disorders as conditions that interfere with normal sleep pattern and quality. A 2016 American College of Physicians guideline defines chronic insomnia as a sleep disorder that causes significant functional distress or impairment at least 3 nights a week for 3 months. DSM-5 summarizes diagnostic features listed below in Table 2.

list.listitem: In primary care, prevalence for chronic insomnia was 19%.
More common in women, especially with advancing age.
Insomnia may be a primary or secondary disorder (see Differential Diagnosis table).
Insomnia is often associated with and secondary to an underlying condition such as depression, anxiety, and/or other underlying medical illnesses.

A small RCT (n=126) published in 2024 compared CBT-I, trazodone, and placebo for chronic hemodialysis patients with insomnia. Both at short-term (7 weeks) and long-term (25 weeks) follow-ups, neither CBT-I nor trazodone showed significant improvement in Ithe nsomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores over placebo, indicating a lack of efficacy in this particular patient population. Notably, the trazodone group experienced a significantly higher frequency of serious adverse events--particularly serious cardiovascular events--raising safety concerns for its use in treating insomnia among hemodialysis patients.
Insomnia is characterized by difficulty in falling asleep, difficulty in maintaining sleep, and/or poor quality of sleep. C
Most patients do not require diagnostic testing. Consider polysomnography if obstructive sleep apnea or periodic limb movement disorder is suspected. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Limb movements start after falling asleep and arouse from sleep
Otherwise healthy individuals, sleep <7 hours with no complaints
History revealing pain preventing sleep initiation
History of caffeine, tobacco, alcohol, illegal and prescribed drugs

list.listitem: Criteria for the diagnosis of insomnia are shown in and .
See separate chapters on obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy, and restless leg syndrome.
Review the history for chronic medical conditions associated with insomnia.
Review the social history and medication list for any substances known to affect sleep initiation or sleep quality.
Assess the patient for the presence of psychiatric illness such as depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder, which may have insomnia as a symptom.
Evaluate for acute changes to sleep or work schedule, and evaluate for acute stressors.
Recommend a sleep log that records sleep hygiene behaviors such as alcohol or food consumption, caffeine use (including in chocolate), liquid consumption, and other activities.
Assess daytime functional impairment by using a sleepiness scale such as the Epworth Sleepiness Scale or the Insomnia Severity Index
Insomnia can be associated with suicidal ideation, consider further evaluation as indicated.
Insomnia is a common complaint in perimenopausal women, consider further evaluation as clinically indicated.

If the cause of insomnia is not obvious from the history, an overnight sleep study (polysomnography) may be used to evaluate the patient for an underlying sleep disorder, such as obstructive sleep apnea or narcolepsy. Other indications for polysomnography include any patient with sleep-related breathing disorders, periodic limb movements, when the diagnosis is uncertain, or if initial treatment fails.
If narcolepsy is suspected, consider the multiple sleep latency test to confirm diagnosis and/or assess the response to treatment.
If trying to confirm total sleep and wake time, actigraphy (a device worn on the wrist) may be used.
Diagnosis is usually made by the history, applying criteria in and .
Always consider the effect of medications and social history.
Cognitive behavioral therapy is the recommended initial treatment for patients with chronic insomnia, including those with chronic disease.A

Dual orexin receptor antagonists (lemborexant, suvorexant, daridorexant) have evidence of efficacy in treating insomnia for up to 3 months, although lemborexant has also shown efficacy at 6 months. A, , , , , These medications may be more efficacious and tolerable than other available pharmacologic treatments, B but are asociated with adverse effects that mimic narcolepsy (excessive daytime sleepiness and sleep paralysis). A

Sedative hypnotics (zolpidem, ramelteon, zaleplon, eszopiclone) are moderately effective in the short-term but may also have adverse effects such as depression and rebound insomnia, especially for the elderly. A

Antidepressants such as trazodone and doxepin have commonly been used off-label for insomnia, although evidence supporting their benefit is limited and their safety/tolerability when used for insomnia is uncertain. B
Melatonin is particularly effective for patients with jet lag and shift-work-related sleep disorders. A

The 2023 European Insomnia Guideline prioritizes cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I). However, pharmacologic therapy may be considered through shared decision-making when CBT-I proves ineffective or is not accessible. The guideline supports the short-term use of benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists for up to 4 weeks, and dual orexin receptor antagonists for up to 3 months. For individuals older than 55, prolonged-release melatonin can be considered for up to 3 months. Low-dose antidepressants are also mentioned as an option for up to 4 weeks, albeit with a weaker recommendation. Any extension of these treatments beyond the recommended durations should be individualized, weighing the potential risks and benefits carefully. The guideline advises against the use of antihistamines, antipsychotics, immediate-release melatonin, ramelteon, and plant-based remedies to treat insomnia.

An evidence-linked practice guideline released in 2016 by the American College of Physicians recommends reserving pharmacologic therapy as second-line treatment (after discussion of risks and benefits) for patients with chronic insomnia in whom cognitive behavioral therapy is unsuccessful. No specific medications were recommended, but the evidence for benefit of benzodiazepines, melatonin, or trazodone in insomnia treatment was concluded to be insufficient.

In 2017, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine published a clinical practice guideline for the pharmacologic treatment of chronic insomnia in adults based on a systematic review and meta-analysis. A "weak" (GRADE) recommendation was given for the use of suvorexant, benzodiazepine receptor agonists, benzodiazepines, ramelteon, and doxepin based on low-quality evidence. The authors also gave a "weak" (GRADE) recommendation against the use of trazodone, tiagabine, diphenhydramine, melatonin, tryptophan, and valerian based on the task force's judgment of an unfavorable benefit/harm ratio.

The dual orexin receptor antagonists lemborexant and daridorexant may be more effective and tolerable than Z-drugs (ex. zolpidem), melatonin receptor agonists, and antidepressants according to a 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis.

A systematic review and network meta-analysis found that while many pharmacologic interventions are effective, they come with significant adverse effects. They conclude that while eszopiclone and lemborexant were effective for long-term use, eszopiclone caused substantial adverse effects and lamborexant had inconclusive safety data. These findings support guideline recommendations to keep these medications as second line.

Zolpidem (Ambien) has been studied for as long as 6 months in patients with chronic primary insomnia. In a study of 669 patients, those given extended release zolpidem 12.5 mg rated the primary endpoint of "helped me sleep" favorably more often than those given placebo (92% vs 60%; NNT = 3). Anxiety, somnolence, and dizziness appeared to be more common in the treatment group (NNH = 27-35), although statistical significance was not reported.

Zaleplon (Sonata) is an effective hypnotic and caused less rebound insomnia than zolpidem in a manufacturer sponsored study. However, in a crossover study, patients were more likely to prefer zolpidem than zaleplon.
Ramelteon (Rozerem) is mildly effective for insomnia characterized by difficulty falling asleep; it decreases sleep latency anywhere from 10 to 19 minutes.,

Eszopiclone (Lunesta) has been shown to reduce sleep onset latency by 12 minutes, decrease wake time after sleep onset by 17 minutes, and increase total sleep time by 28 minutes when compared to placebo in a Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 RCTs with 4372 participants. Adverse events more common with eszopiclone included unpleasant taste (NNH = 5.6), dry mouth (NNH = 25), somnolence (NNH = 25), and dizziness (NNH = 33.3). Eszopiclone plus escitalopram is more effective than escitalopram alone in patients with comorbid anxiety disorder and insomnia (NNT = 7). Eszopiclone is also effective for insomnia in perimenopausal and menopausal women based on patient self-report of sleep quality and duration, with fewer awakenings for hot flushes.

In a small pragmatic placebo-controlled trial with 78 patients, mirtazapine and amitriptyline each significantly improved sleep quality but only for the first 6 weeks. Mirtazapine resulted in recovery from insomnia, but only for the first 6 weeks. There were no meaningful improvements in daytime fatigue or other measures of sleep impact.
In a small (n=60) 6-week RCT in older adults, mirtazapine improved sleep compared with placebo, but nearly 25% of the adults discontinued taking the drug because of adverse effects.

Harms: Non-benzodiazepine sedative hypnotics have been associated with an increased risk of fractures and injury in the elderly based on a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational data. A meta-analysis of studies of zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone, and ramelteon found an increased risk of depression (2.0% vs 0.9%; NNT = 91) in patients taking these drugs. A meta-analysis of the same drugs in older patients also found a significantly increased risk of adverse events.
Three dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) are currently FDA-approved for use in insomnia: lemborexant, suvorexant, and daridorexant.

Lemborexant and daridorexant may be more effective and tolerable than Z-drugs (ex. zolpidem), melatonin receptor agonists, and antidepressants according to a 2023 systematic review and network meta-analysis. Compared to these drug classes, DORAs were found to be better at improving wake time after sleep onset (WASO) and sleep efficiency (SE). Compared to MRAs, they were also better at improving sleep latency (SL). Suvorexant was not shown to have good tolerability compared to placebo.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 high-quality RCTs assessing the clinical safety and narcolepsy-like symptoms of dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs) in insomnia patients identified a higher incidence of treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) with DORAs compared to placebo (RR 1.69; 95% CI, 1.49-1.92). Importantly, DORAs did not significantly increase the risk of TRAEs leading to treatment discontinuation or serious TRAEs. The study highlighted a significant elevation in narcolepsy-like symptoms, specifically excessive daytime sleepiness (RR 2.15; 95% CI 1.02-4.52) and sleep paralysis (RR 3.40; 95% CI 1.18-9.80) associated with DORAs. Individually, suvorexant was associated with the highest relative risk for excessive daytime sleepiness, whereas lemborexant showed the highest risk of the secondary outcomes of somnolence and fatigue.

A meta-analysis of the DORA suvorexant included four RCTs involving 3076 patients with primary insomnia, and was associated with significant improvements in subjective time to sleep onset, subjective total sleep time, and subjective quality of sleep at 1 month and 3 month follow up. The most common adverse effects included somnolence, fatigue and abnormal dreams. Comparative effectiveness trials are needed.

An industry-sponsored double-blinded RCT (SUNRISE 2) enrolled 949 adults aged ≥ 18 years with insomnia and randomized them to placebo, lemborexant 5mg nightly, or lemborexant 10mg nightly. At 6 months, a statistically-significant reduction from baseline in subjective sleep onset latency was seen with lemborexant 5 mg (median -21.8 min) and lemborexant 10 mg (median -28.2 min), compared to placebo (p<0.0001). There were also statistically-significant improvements in delaying the time to first awakening (-46.8 min in lemborexant 5 mg group, -42.0 min in lemborexant 10 mg group) and increase in subjective total sleep time (70.0 min in lemborexant 5 mg group, 74.1 min in lemborexant 10 mg group). These benefits were seen after one week of treatment and were sustained for 12 months. The most common adverse effects were nasopharyngitis, somnolence, and headache. Severe or serious adverse events were reported in 11% of the lemborexant 5 mg group, and in 6% of the lemborexant 10 mg group, but the details of these events were not reported. There were no deaths during the study. Discontinuation rates after 12 months were less than 10%. There was no evidence of rebound insomnia or withdrawal after discontinuation.

SUNRISE 1, another industry-sponsored RCT compared lemborexant 5 mg and 10 mg with placebo and zolpidem tartrate extended relase 6.25 mg in older adults with insomnia. The trial enrolled 1006 adults age 55 and older (median age 63 years) and 86.4% of subjects were women. Both doses of lemborexant resulted in an approximately 20 minute reduction in time to sleep onset as measured by polysomnography, which was a stastistically significant decrease relative to zolpidem ER (7.5 minutes) and placebo (7.9 minutes). The rate of adverse events was similar between lemborexant and zolpidem. This was a short trial of only one month duration which limits its clinical relevance.

The efficacy of daridorexant is based on two industry-sponsored RCTs in 1854 adults (39% ≥65 years old) that demonstrated dose-dependent (50 mg and 25 mg) improvements in wake after sleep onset (WASO), latency to persistent sleep (LPS), and self-reported total sleep time (TST). Compared to placebo, daridorexant 50 mg was associated with mean reductions in WASO of 18 minutes (95% CI, -24 to -13 minutes) and LPS of 12 minutes (95% CI, -16 to -7 minutes), along with a mean increase in TST of 20 minutes (95% CI, 11 to 29 minutes). Daridorexant 25 mg demonstrated more modest improvements in the two studies. Because of its short half-life (8 hours), daridorexant was designed to improve insomnia symptoms while minimizing negative effects of drowsiness and improving daytime functioning. Both the 25 mg and 50 mg doses of daridorexant showed significant improvements in scores on the Insomnia Daytime Symptoms and Impacts Questionnaire (IDSIQ), but these changes may not be clinically significant. Daridorexant appears to be well-tolerated with adverse effects leading to discontinuation occurring in 1-2% in the treatment groups vs. 2% in the placebo group. The most common adverse effects were nasopharyngitis and headache. Falls occurred in less than 1% in the treatment group compared to 3% in the placebo group.

An extension study of the initial 12-week RCTs (n=804) found that daridorexant maintained a favorable safety profile over an additional 40 weeks. There may also be sustained efficacy of daridorexant 50 mg in improving total sleep time and IDSIQ scores. However while promising, these are based on exploratory analyses which should be interpreted with caution.

Benzodiazepines reduce time to fall asleep by about 4 minutes and increase sleep duration by about an hour. However, they increase adverse events (OR 1.8; 95% CI, 1.4-2.4) and daytime drowsiness (OR 2.4; 95% CI, 1.8-3.4). Cognitive behavioral therapy improved success of gradual tapering withdrawal of benzodiazepines in a group of elderly patients with chronic insomnia (70% vs 24%; P <.05; NNT = 2.2).

A Cochrane review identified a modest improvement in subjective sleep quality with the tricyclic antidepressant doxepin and with trazodone as compared to placebo. Evidence for the effectiveness of other antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and other tricyclics for the treatment insomnia is lacking. Additionally, the safety and tolerability of antidepressants for insomnia is uncertain.

A meta-analysis found that melatonin is effective for adults and children with difficulty falling asleep. It helped adults fall asleep 11 minutes faster, and children 17 minutes faster. It is particularly effective in patients with delayed sleep phase disorder (e.g. due to jet lag or shift work), helping those patients fall asleep 39 minutes faster.
However, melatonin is not effective in secondary sleep disorders.

A meta-analysis of 19 studies found that melatonin may improve the quality of sleep, delirium incidence, and ICU length of stay in critically ill patients. However, results of this meta-analysis showed significant heterogeneity, and the evidence was graded as low certainty.

Sustained-release melatonin is effective in weaning chronic insomnia patients from benzodiazepines. In a study of 34 patients, 14 of 18 receiving melatonin were able to discontinue benzodiazepines, compared with 4 of 16 randomized to placebo.

Melatonin has been found effective in several subgroup of patients, including stable schizophrenic patients with insomnia and adults with cognitive impairment. However, a study in asthmatic women found no clinically meaningful benefit.

Nearly 90% of melatonin gummy products analyzed in one study were inadequately labeled. The actual quantity of melatonin ranged from 74% to 347% of the labeled quantity. Similarly, the quantity of CBD ranged from 104% to 118% of the labeled quantity. Be sure to warn parents of the risk of excessive melatonin and CBD ingestion with the gummies.
Tai Chi and low impact aerobics improve sleep in the elderly.

Acupressure - An RCT of 84 patients found that acupressure reduced nocturnal awakenings and wakeful time during sleep more than sham acupressure or placebo. A systematic review of acupuncture found mixed evidence from relatively poor quality studies.
Current evidence is not sufficiently rigorous to support or refute acupuncture as a helpful adjunct in treating insomnia.
A randomized trial of 270 patients concluded that electroacupuncture was more effective than sham acupuncture or usual care in treating insomnia associated with depression.

A randomized trial compared traditional acupuncture, auricular or battlefield acupuncture and usual care for adult cancer survivors with chronic pain and poor sleep. The NNT for both acupuncture groups was 6 for improved sleep compared with usual care (41% and 43% vs 21%).
Bright light therapy has been recommended but clinical trials are lacking.

Multiple meta-analyses have suggested efficacy of various traditional Chinese medicine interventions for insomnia, including Yangxin Anshen Therapy, Long Dan Xie Gan Tang, and Zaoren Anshen capsules. However, the current evidence is heavily limited by a pool of low-quality trials and publication bias, and is therefore insufficient to support or refute its use.
A systematic review of 5 small studies with 288 participants concluded that music therapy may improve sleep quality in older adults.
A systematic review of medical cannabinoids concluded that nabiximols are effective for sleep with moderate to high quality evidence.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended initial treatment for insomnia. A CBT-I is a multimodal therapy that incorporates multiple cognitive and behavioral techniques that are summarized in .

This is true for patients with chronic illness as well. A systematic review found that CBT improved scores for insomnia severity, onset of sleep, and sleeping efficiency, with longer treatment associated with improved scores for sleep efficiency and sleep onset latency. Satisfaction with treatment was high, with only 1 in 8 participants withdrawing from treatment.
An RCT with 188 patients found that for patients receiving CBT, a masked tapering of benzodiazepines by a pharmacist was more effective than letting patients manage it themselves.

Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is typically provided by specialty-trained providers. It may improve sleep outcomes when delivered in the primary care setting by either primary care providers or other health professionals, but more well-designed trials are needed.

In a 2023 open-label randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 642 participants in England, nurse-delivered sleep restriction therapy, a key element of cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), significantly alleviated insomnia severity in primary care settings compared to standard sleep hygiene education, with an adjusted mean difference in Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) scores of -3.0 (95% CI: -3.8 to -2.3) at 6 months. Demonstrating both cost-effectiveness and a favorable safety profile, this intervention may represent a practical and accessible alternative for primary care patients who may not have access to full CBT-I.

A study randomized 327 persons with moderate to severe osteoarthritis and insomnia to telephone based CBT-I or education only. A clinical response as measured by a 30% improvement in an insomnia score occurred more often in the CBT-I group (81% vs 49%, p < .001, NNT = 3).

In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies incorporating at least 3 of the following (cognitive therapy, stimulus control, sleep restriction, sleep hygiene and relaxation training), clinically meaningful improvements were noted in the outcomes of sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, total sleep time and sleep efficiency.

A 2020 VA guideline also endorses CBT for chronic insomnia. The same guideline says sleep hygiene education alone should not be used, and that there is only weak evidence for brief behavioral interventions.
In an RCT, CBT was significantly more effective than relaxation training or placebo. A Cochrane systematic review found that it was effective for patients over 60 years as well.

Chronic primary insomnia responds better to CBT than zopiclone. In an RCT with 46 adults meeting DSM-IV criteria for chronic insomnia, total wake time while attempting to sleep was significantly reduced in the CBT group (52%) at 6 weeks compared with a group taking zopiclone 7.5 mg or placebo. Long-term efficacy was also improved.

A simple intervention of decreasing time in bed (which induces mild sleep deprivation, which enhances the endogenous sleep drive) is associated with improved sleep effectiveness (NNT = 4) in patients with primary insomnia.

In a randomized controlled trial of 303 adults with chronic insomnia, an Internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia program (a 6 week fully automated interactive and tailored web-based program entitled "Sleep Healthy Using the Internet" or SHUTi) was associated with improvements in the insomnia severity index scores, wake after sleep onset, and sleep onset latency.

CBT-I has sustained benefits on insomnia symptoms in patients with heart failure. In a randomized controlled trial of 175 patients with stable HF with preserved or reduced ejection fraction reporting at least mild insomnia symptoms, CBT-I demonstrated sustained improvements in insomnia severity scores, sleep quality, sleep latency, daytime fatigue/sleepiness, as well as six-minute walk distance after 12 months when compared to heart failure self-management (including sleep hygiene education). The trial included patients with mild sleep disordered breathing (apneic-hypopnea index ≤15), which is commonly associated with HF, provided that they were adherent to CPAP therapy.
A systematic review of 4 trials with 191 participants found a large improvement in sleep quality in older adults with a 4 week behavioral intervention program. Sleep time was increased by 25 minutes.
Exercise (although not near bedtime) was found in a systematic review to be effective in the elderly with insomnia.

Encourage good sleep hygiene. Patients should avoid caffeine, nicotine, and alcohol within 4 hours of bedtime; establish regular routines around bedtime, avoid exercise within 4 hours of sleep, sleep only when sleepy, and not take naps.
Other recommendations include not watching the clock, eliminating bedroom clocks, gentle stretching before bed, and avoidance of stimulating late night activities for the elderly.
Avoid use of the bed for activities other than sleep (e.g. television watching, reading, studying, snacking, thinking, planning).
Referral to a sleep specialist is recommended if diagnosis uncertain or if there is strong suspicion of another sleep disorder that would require diagnosis by polysomnography.
Referral may be necessary for cognitive behavioral therapy.
Patients with insomnia are at increased risk for being diagnosed with major depression, panic disorder, and alcohol abuse in the year after diagnosis. B
People with chronic insomnia are more likely to have heart disease, hypertension, breathing problems, chronic pain, and gastrointestinal problems, and urinary problems. B

Use of sedative hypnotics in the elderly increases total sleep time somewhat (mean = 25 minutes) but causes an increase in adverse cognitive events (4.8 times greater than placebo) and adverse psychomotor events (2.6 times over placebo).
Daytime sleepiness is also 3.8 times more likely with sedative hypnotics than with placebo in the elderly.
A systematic review found some benefit of CBT in studies limited to elderly patients. Exercise was also found to be effective in the elderly

A randomized controlled trial of 291 adults aged 60 years or older demonstrated that once-weekly CBT-I for 2 months reduces the risk of incident and recurrent major depression in adults with primary insomnia (12.2% vs. 25.9%, NNT = 7) compared with sleep education therapy.

An RCT of 194 women between 18 and 32 weeks gestation receiving cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia compared to imagery exercises experienced faster and greater reduction in insomnia severity, with a significantly greater likelihood of achieving remission (64% vs 52%, NNT = 8)

The use of zolpidem for greater than 30 days during pregnancy has been associated with an increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes such as low birth weight, preterm birth, small for gestational age, and cesarean section.

feature.caption: Criteria for Sleep Disorder.
feature.feature_body:
A complaint of difficulty initiating sleep, difficulty maintaining sleep or waking up too early, or sleep that is chronically nonrestorative or poor in quality. This sleep difficulty occurs despite adequate opportunity and circumstances for sleep. In addition, at least one of the following forms of daytime impairment related to the nighttime sleep difficulty is reported by the patient:
• Fatigue or malaise
• Attention, concentration, or memory impairment
• Social or vocational dysfunction or poor school performance
• Mood disturbance or irritability
• Daytime sleepiness
• Motivation, energy, or initiative reduction
• Proneness for errors or accidents at work or while driving
• Tension, headaches, or GI symptoms in response to sleep loss
• Concerns or worries about sleep
From Summers MO, Cristosono MI, Stepanski EJ. Recent developments in classification, evaluation, treatment of insomnia. Chest 2006;130:276–286.

feature.caption: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) Insomnia Disorder.

tr.td: A. A predominant complaint of dissatisfaction with sleep quantity or quality, associated with one (or more) of the following symptoms:
Difficulty initiating sleep
Difficulty maintaining sleep, characterized by frequent awakenings or problems returning to sleep after awakenings.
Early-morning awakening with inability to return to sleep
B. The sleep disturbance causes clinically
C. The sleep difficulty occurs at least 3 nights per week
D. The sleep difficulty is present for at least 3 months
E. The sleep difficulty occurs despite adequate opportunity for sleep

F. The insomnia is not better explained by and does not occur exclusively during the course of another sleep-wake disorder (e.g., narcolepsy, breathing-related sleep disorder, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder, parasomnia)
G. The insomnia is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance (e.g., a drug of abuse, a medication)
H. Coexisting mental disorders and medical conditions do not adequately explain the predominant complaint of insomnia
Specifiers:- Episodic - symptoms last at least 1 month but less than 3 months- Persistent - symptoms last 3 months or longer- Recurrent - Two (or more) episodes within the space of 1 year
Sleep Hygiene

Promote healthy behaviors while discouraging negative behaviors: Maintain consistent sleep/wake schedule Avoid stimulants and limit alcohol intake Avoid snoozing and napping Encourage regular exercise
Stimulus Control

Remove non-sleep activities that interfere with sleep and promote behaviors that foster a positive association with the sleep environment: Only go to bed when sleepy Avoid non-sleep activities in the bedroom (e.g. watching TV, reading, smartphone/tablets) Leave the bed if unable to sleep within 20 minutes. Return to bed when sleepy
Sleep Restriction

Limit time in bed to the time spent sleeping and increase gradually as sleep efficiency improves: Restrict time in bed to the average number of hours of a single night's sleep reported in sleep diary Increase time spent in bed by 15-30 minutes if sleep time is >85% of time in bed Maintain fixed wake time regardless of total sleep duration If sleep time is <85% after 10 days, restrict time in bed by additional 15-30 minutes
Relaxation Training
Techniques to reduce muscular tension and arousal in preparation for sleep: Progressive muscle relaxation Guided imagery Paced breathing
Cognitive Therapy
Identify and correct harmful beliefs and attitudes regarding sleep: Overestimation of hours of sleep needed Belief that sleep cannot be controlled Fear of missed opportunities for sleep
Adapted from Buysse DJ. Insomnia. JAMA 2013;309:706–16
